speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER-PROVISIONS OF FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT RESPECTING VALIDITY OF CERTAIN APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On Friday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) rose on a question of privilege, as reported at page 2121 of Hansard, which I think I can summarize. I quote:
My point of privilege is that what we now have is precisely what we had last June. We have the government construing that the Financial Administration Act or regulations made under it gives them authority to do something which the act itself says cannot be done. The Financial Administration Act says that no appointments by the treasury board can be made under it.
The hon. member's statement in this respect is not correct. If hon. members would look at section 5(2) of the Financial Administration Act they would find it provides that the governor in council may authorize the treasury board to exercise all or any of the powers, other than powers of appointment, of the governor in council under the Civil Service Act, the Civil Service Superannuation Act, the Defence Services Pension Act, and parts II to VI of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act.
The action taken was not under any of the foregoing acts, nor was it an "appointment". Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act authorizes the governor in council to make regulations with respect to the conditions under which contracts may be entered into, and it was pursuant to these regulations that the contracts were made. Section 5(2) of the Financial Administration Act has no application whatever to the present situation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE TABLING OF LETTER SUGGESTING MEETING ON JULY 26-27
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies in English and in French of letters which were mailed last Friday to the premiers of the provinces, in which I have suggested it would be valuable to hold an early and preliminary federal-provincial meeting, and I have proposed July 26 and 27 as possible dates for such a meeting.
I should like to inform the house, because it has a bearing on this invitation, as to the government's intentions regarding the conference and the business of the house which is related to it. If a conference can be held on the dates suggested the government will not propose to proceed this week or next week with the second reading of the bill designed to promote employment by financial assistance, in the form of loans with provincial approval, to enable municipalities to augment or accelerate their capital works programs.
The government plans to proceed with the bill during the week following the conference, that is the week of July 29, which could be the last week before the house adjourns. This is legislation which it is urgent to have in force soon so the municipalities can plan their work for this winter with knowledge of the financial assistance for which their representatives have repeatedly asked and which the government believes to be desirable for the encouragement of employment. By proceeding with the bill in two weeks time we


will be acting with the necessary urgency, and we will at the same time make it possible to incorporate in the bill any changes which, in the light of the federal-provincial discussions, the house may think desirable.
At this preliminary conference, Mr. Speaker, the federal government proposes that there should also be discussion of another matter of common interest to Canada and to the provinces, namely pensions. In order to facilitate these discussions it is the government's intention to move on Thursday of this week the resolution concerning legislation for the Canada pension plan. At that time the Minister of National Health and Welfare will give to the house a fuller statement about the government's proposal. There will thus be available the information required for discussion of pension policy by the house, by the public generally and by the provincial governments at the proposed meeting.
It will be the government's intention also to consider with the provinces at this preliminary meeting arrangements for a federal-provincial conference later in the year. This meeting will provide for full discussion of fiscal arrangements and other matters which are of common interest to the provinces and to Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE TABLING OF LETTER SUGGESTING MEETING ON JULY 26-27
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement by the Prime Minister that consultations will now take place with the provinces in respect particularly of the anticipated legislation concerning municipal loans, is one that should have been made before the legislation was introduced at all. Consultation with the provinces does not take place when a government decides on a course and places legislation on the order paper; and then when objection is raised by a premier or premiers, however powerful they may be, the government finds that it must retreat from a position previously taken. However, I suppose consultation, whether early or late, ought to be welcomed as evidence on the part of the government that it realizes now it was in the wrong when it proceeded as it did.
Second, with regard to the pension legislation, I suggest that if there is any need of co-operation on the part of the provinces then the government might consider doing something that has been generally requested by old age pensioners across Canada. If there is any question as to the degree to which this legislation can be implemented without provincial assistance and co-operation; if there is any difficulty in that connection, it has been widely suggested that the government might bifurcate this bill and introduce immediately the provision for the $10 per

month increase in the old age pension. Then, in view of the ever increasing cost of living, the old age pensioners would not have to wait until autumn or until next winter.
However, in summary I say that repentance is good for the soul, and the government having decided on consultation, something that was suggested by hon. members in the official opposition, that is naturally appreciated even though it is late.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE TABLING OF LETTER SUGGESTING MEETING ON JULY 26-27
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regarding the announcement which the Prime Minister has just made to the house, 1 believe he and all of us realize that if there could have been the proper consultation with the provinces before these resolutions were introduced he probably would have avoided the problems which are being faced right now. There is certainly a great deal of urgency in regard to the municipal development and loan fund legislation, and I am sure if the provinces are permitted to carry out the regulations under the resolution which the government has placed before us there will be co-operation from all the provinces.
There is also a certain amount of urgency in regard to the national pension scheme. It relates to the portability of pensions and to the financial arrangements. Again we must realize, particularly at this point in the history of Canada's development that none of these things can be carried on without complete consultation with the provinces, which we in this party trust will come about as a result of the conference which the Prime Minister has called.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE TABLING OF LETTER SUGGESTING MEETING ON JULY 26-27
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that members of this group will welcome the Prime Minister's announcement that a meeting with the premiers is to be held to discuss the municipal development and loan fund legislation. This legislation was introduced with great fanfare. The municipalities were told how much this would help them in solving the unemployment problem and planning their work for next winter. It is, therefore, most important that it be passed as early as possible.
It is a great pity that there was not consultation with the provinces prior to the introduction of this legislation, but I do want to compliment the Prime Minister on stating that after the conference with the premiers has been held he does intend to proceed, and he is not going to allow any obstruction to be placed in the way of proceeding with legislation which is highly desirable and greatly needed in this country.
I am sure the Prime Minister does not want the 60 days of decision to be followed
Dominion-Provincial Relations with 60 days of derision, and this is what will happen unless this important piece of legislation is proceeded with at an early date.
With reference to the pension legislation, we in this group have been urging for some time that if there is going to be any delay in proceeding with the legislation-and we hope there will be the minimum of delay- certainly the government can have no fears at all about proceeding with the $10 a month increase in the old age security pension. That at least would be an interim step, and there is no reason for it to wait until constitutional problems have been worked out with the provinces. So far as this group are concerned we would be prepared to proceed on that basis, by separating the increase in the old age security pension from the Canada pension plan.

subtopic: D.E.W. LINE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DISCONTINUANCE OF SOME STATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: D.E.W. LINE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF DISCONTINUANCE OF SOME STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1955 Canada and the United States signed an agreement for the establishment of the distant early warning line on Canadian territory as part of a comprehensive North American control and warning system. This agreement was announced in the House of Commons on May 20, 1955.
Recently the United States government suggested to the Canadian government that a reappraisal of the effectiveness of the D.E.W. line indicates that certain adjustments may be made in the equipment configuration and still provide acceptable early warning. The new configuration would permit the discontinuance of 28 of the smaller D.E.W. line stations.
The Canadian government has agreed to the United States government's plan and the necessary arrangements are being made by the authorities of both governments. The affected facilities will be disposed of in accordance with existing agreements between the two governments.
Twenty intermediate D.E.W. line stations located in Canada, and eight in Alaska, will be closed. Approximately 123 Canadian and 60 United States citizens will be affected by this action. They are employees of the Federal Electric Co., Paramus, New Jersey, which has a United States air force contract for the operation and maintenance of the D.E.W. line.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CERTAIN AUTHORIZED EXPENDITURES FOR FISCAL YEAR 1962-63

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minisler of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CERTAIN AUTHORIZED EXPENDITURES FOR FISCAL YEAR 1962-63
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-86, for approving certain expenditures authorized for the public service, and the application of certain amounts in the accounts, for the financial year ended the 31st March, 1963.
Mr. E. J. Benson (Parliamentary Secretary
to Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to close the accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1963. This action is necessary in order that the audit of the accounts may be completed and reported upon by the Auditor General. His report will then, of course, be submitted to the public accounts committee where witnesses may be called and hon. members of the committee may fully examine the accounts, along with the report thereon submitted by the Auditor General. The Auditor General will, in his report, comment upon any actions which he may believe open to question.
Bill C-86 will be the final appropriation act for the fiscal year 1962-63. Parliament was dissolved on February 6, 1963, without having completed its consideration of the estimates and without having made adequate provision for the expenditures for the complete year 1962-63.
I will not comment upon the fact that vast sums of money were spent during the 1962-63 fiscal year without departmental estimates having been approved by this house. I believe that this matter was amply debated both in the house during the last parliament and during the ensuing election campaign.
I respectfully suggest to hon. members that this bill be dealt with as expeditiously as possible in order that the Auditor General may complete his job for last year and that we may get on with this year's business, to assure that a similar situation does not occur in the current fiscal year.
The situation experienced in February, 1963 was to all intents and purposes an exact parallel to the situation following from the dissolution of parliament in February, 1958. With minor exceptions the procedure which this government intends to follow in cleaning up the outstanding business of 1962-63 will parallel the course of action pursued by the former government in August and September, 1958, in cleaning up the outstanding business of 1957-58. It should be noted, too, that a major portion of the action currently being proposed is not open to question on this occasion, as it might have been in 1958 and prior years, inasmuch as an amendment to
15, 1963
Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 the Financial Administration Act, passed by parliament late in 1958, requires that amounts appropriated by way of special governor general's warrants while parliament is not in session must be submitted for consideration by parliament during the ensuing session.
As in 1958, the government has provided a report on supply for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1963, in which is set forth in great detail the total estimates and supply picture for 1962-63. On Friday last, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, I tabled this report on supply which set forth for each vote the total of all of the estimates, both tabled and not tabled, which were approved by the government in respect of 1962-63. There was also a comparable presentation of the amounts of supply already granted or to be granted in respect of the past fiscal year, including the amounts authorized by appropriation acts, the amounts authorized in pursuance of governor general's warrants, and the amounts for which authority is being requested in this bill. In this latter category there are 36 items which are considered to be proper charges to the 1962-63 budgetary accounts. None of these items, when authorized by this bill, will provide for further cash outlays chargeable to the old year accounts.
The summary on page 3 of the report discloses that the total amount of all items to be voted-that is government expenditures other than those which are payable under continuing statutory authority-amounted to $4,293,642,685. All but $328 million of that total amount was included in estimates tabled during the last session of parliament. There is here a difference between the 1958 and 1963 experiences. The final supplementaries for 1957-58 were tabled before parliament dissolved on February 1, 1958, whereas the final supplementaries for 1962-63 were not tabled prior to dissolution on February 6, 1963.
The summary discloses further that parliament passed five appropriation acts in 1962, thereby appropriating $3,390.7 million, leaving $902.8 million of the estimates unauthorized at the point of dissolution. Subsequently the Governor General, under the emergency authority contained in section 28 of the Financial Administration Act, caused special warrants to be issued authorizing further expenditures of $641.3 million.
Here is the second point of difference between the practice followed in 1958 and that of 1963. Five years ago the government proposed, and the Governor General approved, a single warrant to provide for expenditures during the last two months of 1957-58. This year a two phased exercise, resulting in the issue of warrants on February 8 and March 4, allowed for a more careful review of actual cash requirements, and it is hoped that the final

Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 audit for 1962-63 will indicate a more careful use of special warrant authority in 1963 than was the case five years ago.
The final entry on the summary relates to the proposal that parliament now authorize the charging to the budgetary accounts of 1962-63 of certain expenditures deemed to be appropriate subjects for such treatment. This treatment, in most cases, accords with that afforded in 1958. In other cases items are suggested for inclusion in order to overcome obvious inconsistencies in the 1958 exercise; and finally, some items are proposed on their individual merits. A basic rule in the choice of the 36 items for which parliamentary authority is now requested was that the relevant cash outlays had already been made and that no new cash outlays, chargeable to the 1962-63 accounts, will result from their being authorized during this session. I will be pleased to answer questions on these items during the committee stage of this bill.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the summary indicates that some $49.7 millon of the total estimates to be voted was not ultimately required. Most of this amount represents those portions of appropriations which would lapse in the normal course of events. A footnote to the summary provides a balancing entry for those who may be interested in reconciling last year's records respecting appropriation acts with the figures shown in this report.
I would now refer the house to page 4 and onward of the report. Here we find, for each vote in each department, both the total estimates amount and the comparable supply amount. The supply amount is also broken down into its important components, namely the portion provided by parliament during 1962, the portion made available by special governor general's warrants, and the amount which parliament will now be asked to authorize.
Returning now to the bill which is before the house, this bill proposes approval of the expenditures authorized by the aforementioned governor general's warrants and the 36 special items which have not yet been authorized but which are considered to be proper charges to the budgetary accounts of the fiscal year 1962-63. Because no final supply bill for 1962-63 has yet been passed, this bill has been prepared in a form which will serve as a final 1962-63 supply bill in Canadian financial records. Finally, as the passage of this measure will not in any way restrict the authority of the public accounts committee to pursue its normal activities in respect of the public accounts for 1962-63, I urge that it be given favourable consideration by this house.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, it has occurred to me that I should forestall
any arguments which may be made that expenditures for the fiscal year 1962-63 have in any way been increased beyond what is normal and proper. Hon. members will note that on page 71 of the report on accounts the total amount of the 36 items for which authority is sought is shown as $211,856,066. Considering this amount, if one then looks at pages 67 to 70 of the report they will see items amounting to $37,545,558 which do not affect the budgetary deficit. This reduces the amount which is being added, which would affect the deficit to $174,310,508. Of this there are items which are identical or directly similar to items included in 1958-that is, items which were put into the final supply bill in 1958 by the former government-in the amount of $73,529,057. This includes items such as the agricultural commodities stabilization account loss of $71,856,049, and so on, totalling $73,529,057. This reduces the amount which could be considered as affecting the budgetary deficit to $100,781,451. From this there should be deducted two items which were covered by governor general's warrants in 1958 and which are now being included as a final supply item in 1963. These are first of all the Canadian National Railways deficit, which is $48,919,500, and the final payment with respect to the Colombo plan in the amount of $3,458,333. Thus if we deduct this amount of $52,377,833 we get down to an amount of $48,403,618 as affecting the budgetary deficit due to this bill and to the actions of the government.
From this there is a certain group of other items which I believe are quite proper charges and which I would deduct at this point. First of all there is the T.C.A. deficit, which is included in this supply bill, of $3,540,700, which occurred in the calendar year 1962 and is thus, I believe, a proper charge to the 1962-63 fiscal year. There are also several items to effect write-offs which were recognized as valid prior to March 31, 1963. These include the write-off of the N.R.U. reactor of $25,239,005, the write-off of loans to Northern Canada Power Commission, which was doing some work at Inuvik in the Northwest Territories, for which the government had agreed to reimburse it. This amounts to $7,004,000. Then there is the write-off of land in the canal navigation system at Cornwall, Ontario, which was recommended in two succeeding years by the Auditor General, amounting to $1,710,600; and the write-off of loans to the New Westminster harbour commission of $284,700, making in total a further reduction of $37,779,005.
This gets the amount that would affect the deficit and is debatable down to $10,624,613, and this is made up of the following items.


Payments in connection with the winter works program of 1962-63, the final cost being $5 million, and payments to various funds to which there was a contribution by the government to bring these funds up to the agreed amount, as follows: the national gallery fund, the national centennial fund, the national library purchase account, the national capital fund and the railway crossing grading account. These amount to $1,043,291. Then there is the payment with regard to the south Saskatchewan dam, affecting 1962-63, of $240,259. There are certain reimbursements to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which the government agreed to make with respect to the past fiscal year. The amount in respect of research and community planning of C.M.H.C. was $754,794; reimbursement of C.M.H.C. for losses in federal-provincial housing projects in the past fiscal year amounted to $1,204,949; reimbursement of C.M.H.C. for forgiveness of municipal loans under section 36G of the National Housing Act for 1962-63 amounted to $1,873,630. Finally the figure in regard to dredging Montreal harbour, which work was completed in the fiscal year 1962-63, amounted to $507,700. This gives a total of $10,624,613.
I think all hon. members will agree that these are proper charges to the accounts for the fiscal year 1962-63, and I would therefore urge all hon. members to assist in allowing
the passage of this bill in order to clean up last year's accounts.

Mr. Speaker, I think first I should congratulate the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance on the way he is piloting this bill through the house. It is always a pleasure to see young members coming along and those who are not always in the front row given responsibilities in piloting bills through certain stages. I want to congratulate the parliamentary secretary in this regard.
Having said that, I was reminded in listening to him of something Shakespeare once wrote; "Methinks the lady doth protest too much". If the bill is as simple as he says it is and as clearcut as all that with no ulterior motive whatsoever, then I do not know why he spent ten minutes of his time in dealing with anticipated criticism which might be made in committee. I will not say he had a guilty conscience, sir, but there might have been an uneasy feeling in his mind when he began to deal with the figures which are presently before us.
There is, of course, nothing one can do about these figures at the moment because we have no way in which we can balance

One has to accept, and one does accept, of course, the statement of the parliamentary secretary in respect to the way in which these moneys have been advanced and expended. I quite agree with him that there were no additional items here which could go into the cash balance of the public account other than those loans and advances to which he referred which are below the line. But there are quite a few figures, Mr. Speaker, included in those to which he referred which do affect the increased deficit or the budgetary deficit of the country.
If I were a suspicious person, which of course I am not; and if I were a partisan, which of course I am not, I might feel that possibly the parliamentary secretary found some way of adding figures to these expenditures so as to show how much bigger the deficit under the preceding government, the government of my right hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), was compared with that of the present government. I am sure that when these figures were brought down the thought was that it would be very helpful if it could be shown that the deficit incurred by the preceding government was substantially greater than the deficit which would be incurred by this government under the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) on June 13.
Now, of course, as things have turned out the government know that is entirely hopeless, and what they are hoping to do is to have the deficit of the present government under the Minister of Finance, if possible, not too much greater than the deficit incurred by the preceding government. The situations have been reversed. But I think that even with these additions, which perhaps can be questioned and to which I will make some brief reference in passing in committee, the purpose has failed. It would be indulging in the rankest of prophecy to say that the deficit next year might be much more substantial than the deficit this year if we completely accept without question all the figures contained in the white paper and the figures contained in this report on supply. We do not accept them per se, Mr. Speaker. We do not think some of them should be properly charged to the preceding government at all. However, I will have something to say about them in a moment-and one does not have to apologize for this-and in committee we may question certain items which are before us.
One reason you have no starting point and no way in which to balance them is that in the estimates we have before us, in the first

Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 column of the total estimates in the report, you will find the words "excluding statutory items". Mr. Speaker, I am not quarrelling with those words entered there. They were entered there, as the parliamentary secretary said, in the report which my predecessor the former minister of finance brought down in 1958. But when you bring those words in, what is meant by statutory items? Where is the starting point? For instance, everyone knows that the salary, shall we say, of Mr. Speaker is fixed by statute. We know what the salary is; it is easy to determine. But when you come to another statutory item, such as the amounts paid to the provinces, then how do you determine those amounts without going into all the details with officials? Because the amount paid to each province varies from year to year, depending on the shift in population of the province concerned. How do you determine another statutory item such as the amount paid by way of family allowances? That amount varies too with the population. How do you determine, as another example, the amounts paid to the universities? That is a statutory amount, and it too depends upon the population of each province.
So there is no way whatsoever of determining these amounts by taking these figures per se, analysing them, and coming to any final result in so far as they affect the total over-all deficit. All we have here is the amount of our appropriation acts passed by the preceding parliament and the amount covered by governor general's warrants, and we are asked today to pass 36 items amounting in all to $211 million. We are also asked to approve the fact that the preceding government spent this money before March 31 or, if they did not spend it, that they were responsible for its expenditure.
Mr. Speaker, one could spend days and days and days analysing these figures. The minister could have his officials in front of him and one could go through one department after another, and in the end you would reach a result depending on your own wishes and on the imagination you were using in analysing the figures. So we of the opposition do not propose to spend very much time this afternoon in dealing with the bill on second reading. Some of the items to which the parliamentary secretary referred should undoubtedly be charged to the expenditures of last year. The C.N.R. deficit-although on this I will have some comment to make when we reach committee stage-and the T.C.A. deficit are both matters properly chargeable to the former government under the fiscal year ending March 31.
But there are others. I question entirely the figure relating to the N.R.U. reactor. The re-

actor has not been thrown down the drain. It is still working and still doing the same work today as it did a year ago. There is no reason in the world why that reactor should be charged up to our expenditure for last year except for the fact that the government wants to increase the deficit by some $20 million plus. With regard to the Cornwall canal, the parliamentary secretary said this had been recommended by some committee some years ago. Is that any reason why it should be charged up to the former government at this particular time? Mr. Speaker, you know very well why it is being charged up. As I say, one could go on and on with various items, and I do not propose to do so. But I think, or I hope, we will spend a brief time, subject to other hon. members in the committee, dealing with some of the items, and then we will let the matter pass.
I should like to point out in passing, Mr. Speaker, that if you accept the deficit as now proposed by the parliamentary secretary of $709 million-we do not, of course, but for the sake of argument if we accept it-we find it is $82 million less than the actual deficit in the preceding year. So that even accepting the figure of $709 million the deficit is $82 million less than it was the previous year. One would have liked to see it even less. We can argue that it should be less, but even accepting the figure as it is one can say that the government of which I had the pleasure and honour of being a member did keep its promise and worked, although perhaps very slowly, toward a balanced budget.
When you think, Mr. Speaker, of some of the expenditures made by the former government as compared with the previous one, the actual increase in expenditures on the figures before us today is $64 million over the preceding year 1962. One could analyse these figures and see how they were arrived at. I can point out right away, though, that during the past year the government of which I was a member paid out for technical training and vocational schools $171 million more than was paid out in the preceding year. I have forgotten the exact figure, but there were millions and millions of dollars more paid out in health and welfare fields than were disbursed in the preceding year. We could argue about the deficit, that we should not have increased the deficit and so on. The fact remains that last year the interest and carrying charges on our debt was $79 million more than in the preceding year. When one realizes that our total increase in expenditure was only $62 million and that those two items to which I have referred amounted in themselves to $240 million, we can certainly suggest without boasting that there was very good administration shown in carrying on

the services which we did carry on while incurring such a relatively small increase.
I hope the parliamentary secretary can tell us, when we get into committee, what was the increase in the statutory payments during the past year as compared with the year before. I think hon. members will find that it was fairly substantial. We know from our records that people are living longer, that more and more money is being paid out to those in receipt of old age pensions, fortunately for those of us who are getting older. I suspect that the statutory payments made last year were a good many millions of dollars more than were paid out the year before. I am suggesting, without taking the time of the house by going into the figures in great detail, that even having regard to the amounts which are now before us, we are relatively happy with the record so established. It is certainly not one which suggests poor administration or anything of that kind as far as the government of which I was a member is concerned.

I should like to give the house an example of the former government's indifference to the rights of parliament. On page 61 of the report on supply we find an item of $16 million in respect of which authority is now being sought. The item concerns payments under the Freight Rates Reduction Act. Not one cent of that sum was appropriated by way of interim supply or authorized by an appropriation act. I know there were a number of members who were anxious to discuss this question whenever it might have arisen, either during the discussion on interim supply or on some other occasion. The opinion is definitely prevalent in this country that this direct grant discriminates against forms of transport other than the railways. We in this group particularly wanted the opportunity to discuss this matter and the effects of such an appropriation, before the money was spent. Now it is spent.
As I say, I do not wish to take up much of the time of the house at this point, but I believe we must take a long, hard look at what is happening to these important rights and privileges of hon. members in all parts of the house. In my humble opinion we should have the right to control the purse strings and governments must not put other considerations, whatever they may be, above this important duty which falls on hon. members.
There is another matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. I wish to raise it again when we get into committee. On page 8 we see an amount of $71,856,049 for which there does not appear to be any authorization by interim supply or by special warrant of the Governor General. This amount is all being asked for under the bill before us now, and we should like to

Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 have a detailed explanation as to the purpose for which this $71 million is required.
As I have said, when one looks at these expenditures one feels a certain amount of futility. The money has already been spent. It is gone. What is the use, therefore, of raising any objections now? This is the situation we face. I know that the trucking industry, for example, had a lot of representations to make to the government respecting the $16 million that was paid to the railways. They seem to think they can prove that this money and other money that the government grants to the railways is used to lower freight rates in certain areas so as to squeeze out the trucking industry.
I am certain that the government and members of parliament generally do not wish to appropriate public funds for the purpose of squeezing certain segments of industry out of business, in this instance by giving the railways subsidies which enable them to lower their rates below what is reasonably competitive.
With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to your attention again that the responsibility of government includes the responsibility to organize the business of the house so that the rights and privileges of members respecting the spending of money will not be taken away.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CERTAIN AUTHORIZED EXPENDITURES FOR FISCAL YEAR 1962-63
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to validate expenditures that were made in the fiscal year 1962-63. It is fairly evident that the house has no option but to pass the bill, but I suggest that while we are doing so the flag ought to be put at half mast. We are in effect drawing attention to the fact, and it is a fact that the bill does not set aside, that the 1962-63 fiscal year was one in which all the taxpayers' money that was spent was spent without consideration of the items in the estimates.
A very large portion of the money got voted through the medium of interim supply bills. Every time an interim supply bill was presented to the house we were assured that no one of these bills was appropriating all of any estimate for the year, and that there would be an opportunity to members before the entire amount was voted to discuss the individual items. Hon. members who were here will recall that in December of last year I pointed out that the undertaking given at that time by the then minister of finance was in my view an undertaking that was given in good faith but one that would not be kept. And it was not.
The other way in which money was authorized for expenditure was by the issue of governor general's warrants. Yet even


though it can be said that the money spent under the interim supply bills and by governor general's warrants was spent legally, it is still true that in that year, 1962-63, the House of Commons of Canada, the peoples' representatives, the members who are supposed to have control of the purse strings, had no opportunity to vote for any one of the individual items of the estimates. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that my proposal that the flag be put at half mast is a very mild one. This is something that is not good in the history of Canadian parliamentary democracy. To have this kind of experience is sad.
The bill before us will do three things at least, though it might do more as well. It does a certain amount of bookkeeping and this leads, of course, to argument between the present government and the former minister of finance as to which column figures are being put in. It does not make much difference to the taxpayer in the end. As I say, the bill does some bookkeeping. The second thing it does is to give formal or parliamentary approval to the money that was spent under the terms of governor general's warrants. The third thing it does is to authorize the expenditure of the 36 items referred to by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. But in any case, Mr. Speaker, no matter under what heading you subsume the various items, in all cases we are talking about money that is already spent, and there is nothing we can do about it but note the fact that the year 1962-63 was a sorry one for the parliament of Canada in terms of the responsibility that is supposed to devolve upon the people's representatives.
I know that when this question comes up arguments arise as to whose responsibility it was, whose fault it was. There is no point now in going over all that, except to say that parliament could have been called earlier in 1962. We could have got at the estimates if there had been recognition at that time of their importance, the importance of the principle that parliament controls the purse strings. But I think what the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance said at one point is perhaps something that we should note. He said "Let us not spend too much time quarrelling about the past; let us make sure that it does not happen in this session of parliament". I suggest that is an admonition that is well put. Let it not happen in this session of parliament. It ought not ever to happen again.
I have done a lot of thinking about this problem, Mr. Speaker, and I confess I do not see how we can prevent it from happening by changing the rules or changing the statutes. I think the only way this sort of

thing can be prevented is by increasing in the minds of all members of parliament, and particularly on the part of those who are on the government side of the house at any given time, respect for the rights and traditions of parliament. There is need for more respect for the importance of the control of the purse strings. If a government had that respect I suggest it would find a way to organize the business of the house in such a manner that the estimates would be dealt with.
There is a tendency in this House of Commons to feel that the estimates are something that can be dealt with when everything else is done; that they can be put off until Friday; that we can hold Saturday sittings and deal with estimates, or that they can be left until the fall or some later time in the session. The feeling is that we have to get along with legislation because legislation is important. I am right there with everyone else asking the government to proceed with particular pieces of legislation in which I am interested, but estimates also constitute legislation. They constitute one of the most important pieces of legislation that we deal with, and I hope that the experience we are going through today, realizing that we are put on the spot in that we have to pass a bill about which we can do nothing, will cause us to think a bit about the importance of the role of dealing with the expenditure of money.
As I say, it is a highly perfunctory performance we are going through this afternoon. Members on the government side are now on the treasury benches and they are faced with the constitutional and legal necessity of getting this legislation through. It relates to money they did not spend but because they have to get it through they are prepared, of course, to support the bill. Members of the official opposition are faced with a bill that validates spending done by them last year, so they have got to support it. The other two parties in this corner of the house were witnesses to the whole business. Most of us were here last year and we tried to get the estimates brought on. We wanted a chance to discuss them. We have no option but to support the bill as well, but I emphasize the perfunctory nature of the whole thing not just to throw stones in the direction of those I think were responsible but to urge the necessity of greater respect for the estimates of parliament, greater respect for the principle that parliament does control the purse strings.
In this connection I hope that when the day comes that we get the special committee on procedure established, that committee
Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 will give some thought to this problem. I hope that thought will be given to it in some other quarters. I have been interested in browsing through the records of some of the early years of the House of Commons of Canada, and I have discovered that in the first session of the first parliament, which began after the 1st of July, 1867, the members of that day had a supply bill.
They thought it was a huge sum of money. It was $5 million. Mind you, this amount was not for a full 12 months; it was for nine months from July 1, 1867 to March 31, 1868. This would work out to something in the order of about $6.5 million for a full year.
Perhaps 1867 is not a good year to take as a basis for comparison. Let us move on two or three years to about 1870 or 1871. If you look at the records for those years, you will find that the total expenditures of the Dominion of Canada were running around the order of $13 million or $14 million a year. I am sure our forebears who sat in the House of Commons of that day, the building that was previously here, were impressed by this staggering figure of $13 million per year. This year, Mr. Speaker, our budget is something over $6 billion. We have multiplied our expenditures from 1870 to the present time by 480 times. We have increased our expenditures, in other words, by 48,000 per cent.
However, Mr. Speaker, we are still handling these much larger sums of money in almost the same way as those sums of money were handled in 1867 and 1870. It is still done by the individual items having to be processed through the committee of supply. They managed to do this in eight or ten days back in those days, because the amounts were much smaller. The basic way in which the matter is handled, however, has not changed in all these years.
Now, I have already said something about the importance of parliamentary control of the purse strings, and I think this must not be overlooked in any way, shape or form. I do believe, however, that we have to find some way to cope with the greatly increased amount of money we have to vote, to cope with the greater complexity of government business. One proposal that was suggested a few years ago was that of setting up a standing committee on estimates. It does not seem to me that this method has been used as much as it might have been. I should like to urge that our special committee on procedure, or other bodies that are interested, take another look at that process to see if we cannot make more use of the committee on estimates. This committee was set up on the basis of having the estimates referred to it, with the idea that those estimates would

Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 be returned to the committee of supply, and with the further idea that, having been examined thoroughly in the standing committee, time might be saved in the house.
The idea is not just to save time so that we can go off on a holiday. The fact is that there are only 365 days a year and if we were to sit every day in the year we would not be able to do all the business that comes before us in the same way as it was done by our forebears, even although they had to deal with only 1/480th of the amount of money with which we have to deal.
Perhaps we will have to come to some understanding on a basis whereby we thoroughly examine some departments one year and leave the remainder of the departments to be examined thoroughly the next year. I throw this out as a suggestion. I do not believe we should go on year after year, decade after decade, without finding any new ways of dealing with the problem. The experience through which we are now going should bring us face to face with the fact that this is a very real problem. I know that we have this particular problem because the dissolution that took place and the fact that elections came along pretty thick and fast. However, even when we have a parliament that lasts three, four or five years, this same problem remains, of how to get a proper treatment of the estimates. All that the present experience does is to highlight the problem for us.
I urge that, based on our having to vote today a whole year's estimates without having considered them at all, the time has come when we ought to be trying to find some way to improve our handling of these estimates. I emphasize again that even more important than any changes in the way we handle them, even more important than any rules or committees or what have you, is the need for all of us in this place, having the highest respect for the importance of our job as members of parliament, to see to it that we control the purse strings, that it is not left to the executive to spend money and come along afterwards to get approval. This basic tenet of parliamentary practice should be followed.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to hold up the passage of this bill unduly, but in view of the snipings in which various hon. members have indulged, and which have been directed at the former government because of alleged delay in the passage of legislation and estimates during the 25th parliament, I have a few words to say in reply. I should like, therefore, to take a few moments to go through what I believe are some of the most important


facts arising out of that parliament as they refer to the present situation.
It is very disturbing, for a member who sat through the 25th parliament as a member of the government party, to hear these people who filibustered, delayed and wrangled over the business of the house last year, preventing the passage of a great deal of legislation, saying now that the former government failed to conduct the business of the house in a proper manner. I think that in saying this they are, to say the least, being unfair; and to say the worst, they are wrong. I should like to make some comparisons because I think comparisons are what we must make at this point.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said we must examine the procedures of the house in handling some of these matters. It was stated also that we ought not to allow this situation to happen again, as it did in the 25th parliament-that is the passage of estimates by governor general's warrants without complete investigation by the house. I cannot help agreeing with the hon. member entirely on that point. What is required in order to conduct such a full, fair investigation is a responsible opposition. I am going to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in this 26th parliament we have a responsible opposition, and I refer particularly of course to the official opposition. I want to say that this opposition has acted in the best interest of the country and has proven to be a responsible opposition, trying to do its job for the sake of the country, and actually conducting the business of the house without all the delaying tactics that were used in the last parliament.
Now, in spite of the remarkable number of mistakes the government has made during this session, the progress on essential and non-controversial measures brought before this parliament has been good. This is the 42nd day of this session and we have completed the speech from the throne, and the budget debate, we have passed the exports insurance bill, the bill to establish the Atlantic development board and the department of industry. In so far as estimates are concerned, we have completed the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce and we have made a good start on the estimates of the Department of Transport.
I should like to refer for a moment to private bills because, here again, I believe this parliament has made good progress. Most of us remember that in the last parliament private bills were delayed, and on many occasions for political reasons. In so far as standing committees are concerned, I would refer particularly to banking and commerce and

miscellaneous private bills, in which many of the private bills were opposed merely for the purpose of delay. A good many of these committees were used for the sole purpose of trying to bring some other issues before them, and of trying to delay the passage of government business. Already this session the committee on banking and commerce and the committee on miscelleneous private bills have passed a good many of the private bills left over from the last parliament.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) mentioned that the former government did not succeed in passing the estimates, and he laid some blame on that government. In reply I would say that if his party had not divided when the crucial vote came, we might have been able to finish the business of the house.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CERTAIN AUTHORIZED EXPENDITURES FOR FISCAL YEAR 1962-63
speechtext:
I apologize for detaining the house for a few minutes on this item, but I rise to discuss a matter which I consider to be of primary importance with respect to our national integrity and the future unity of this nation. Before proceeding with my remarks I wish to quote from a book which has been distributed to hon. members. It is entitled, "Organization of the Government of Canada" and it is published by the queen's printer under date of January, 1962. I quote from page 158 with respect to the functions of the Department of External Affairs:
The main functions of the department are the conduct of official relations between Canada and other countries and of Canadian participation in international organizations, and the protection of Canadian interests abroad.
Then, on page 159, I read:
There is also an economic division which deals with all financial, commercial and general economic questions possessing international implications, in co-operation with the departments of finance, trade and commerce and other bodies concerned.
And on the same page:
The legal division advises on questions of international law, including the interpretation of treaties. It is responsible for liaison with the Department of Justice. Besides its general section, it comprises a treaty section, which assists in the preparation of international agreements, and a claims section, which deals with claims of Canadians against foreign countries.
I have discussed this question with some very well informed people and I have had telephone conversations-I get a lot of telephone calls on various questions-and I have had correspondence. I raise this question because I have been requested to do so by some very important people in Canada and by those who are concerned about the actions of this government. I am reliably informed that a former prime minister, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, was most particular with respect to the observance of protocol in the conduct of official relations between Canada and other countries. I am informed he had such strict regard for the recognition of Canada as a sovereign state

and for the sole right of the government of Canada to conduct official relations and negotiations with other countries on any question that, while he consulted with and sought the advice of provincial governments on matters affecting their provinces, he always insisted that officials or representatives of the government of Canada should be the only persons present during negotiations with another country. I am also reliably informed that former prime minister Louis St. Laurent held the same view and insisted on the same practice. I am further advised that in reaching agreement on the St. Lawrence seaway the same practice was followed. Though the provinces were consulted and their wishes considered, the negotiations were carried on by the representatives of the government of Canada.
Indeed, so firmly fixed is the sovereign right of Canada to negotiate treaties and agreements that on several occasions the government of Canada has disallowed provincial legislation on the ground that it affected Canada's relations with other countries, a field which is the prerogative of the federal government, as established by law as well as by practice. For instance, there was some legislation passed at one time by the government of British Columbia with respect to orientals which was disallowed by the federal government on this basis. Later, there was some legislation passed by the government of Manitoba which was disallowed because it was considered an interference with the sovereign right of the government of Canada to deal with any matter affecting its relations with other nations.
I do not know whether hon. members have suspected it or not, but I am coming to a point. I wish to deal with what has happened with regard to the Columbia river treaty. Let me tell the committee what is happening to break down the precedent and practice of former years. Premier Bennett informs the public through the press that Robert Anderson, former secretary in the Eisenhower administration-a man who claimed to have President Kennedy's ear-is his adviser on the Columbia treaty question. In effect, Premier Bennett is telling us that Mr. Anderson is a go-between operating between the government of British Columbia and the government of the United States or its agencies concerned. In the second place, Premier Bennett goes to Washington, it is widely advertised in the press, to negotiate directly with officials of the United States with respect to the Columbia river treaty, or with agencies of the government of the United States on details relating to the Columbia river negotiations, and in particular the price to be paid for power. These matters are the responsibility of the

federal government. They are the responsibility of the federal government according to tradition, precedent and practice. It is this government which should conduct the negotiations, giving effect to the wishes of the province so long as they do not transgress the national interest. When it comes to negotiations between Canada and another country, the federal government must take the responsibility.
What is hapening now has all been done with the obvious, though tacit, agreement of the government of Canada. Without a doubt, in view of the statements made by Premier Bennett to the press, the silence of this government means consent. It is a well known and well established practice that the government of Canada cannot delegate its powers with respect to external affairs or its dealings with foreign nations.
What is the latest act in this drama? We find that recently Mr. Avery Peterson, the United States consul-general in Vancouver, visited the Columbia riding during the provincial by-election. I am informed that while he was there he attended political meetings and took copious notes of what speakers for the New Democratic party and others had to say. He visited around, held conversations with people and all the rest of it. In our opinion, and in the opinion of a good many people, this was in extremely bad taste, especially in view of the particular issue which was concerning the electorate of that riding at that time. His presence was resented by some people including some of the electors. Others considered it a subtle form of influence brought into the campaign at the instigation of Premier Bennett. We object to the use of officials of the American state department to influence the electors of British Columbia in a provincial by-election.
Newspapers use the phrase "Bennett-United States negotiations" and correspondence refers to the same thing. This clearly indicates that a good many people are of the opinion that the government of Canada has surrendered its sovereign rights in this respect and has said to Premier Bennett of British Columbia:	You go ahead and do the
negotiating. We object to this practice.
I will just make reference to the law in the United States. The government of the United States is very jealous of its federal powers and under its constitution no state is permitted to deal with any foreign power. I have looked into the matter and I have the book here, but I am not going to take the time of the house to refer to it. When an ordinary stump rancher starts to wander through legal tomes, Mr. Chairman, he has got a task on his hands, however I spent
Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 yesterday afternoon reading up on this subject. I find that the United States will not tolerate any executive or official of a state government dealing in any manner with any other country. Under the oath of office taken by the executives of state governments they take an oath to the constitution and to abide by this principle, and if they violate that oath of office by overstepping the responsibilities of the state government and transgressing the rights and responsibilities of the federal government they can be impeached.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, first of all the government has departed from the established and recognized procedure and practice in its negotiations with the government of the United States and the government of British Columbia with respect to the Columbia river treaty, and I am not alone in that view. Second, it has by its tacit agreement with Premier Bennett's direct negotiations with officials of the government of the United States or its agencies surrendered its sovereign rights and has violated a principle that has been given effect throughout the years by tradition, by practice and by procedure. Third, by so doing it has established a precedent that will promote the balkanization of Canada and sow the seeds of national disunity in the days ahead. Just imagine if each provincial government, accepting the procedure that has been recognized and accepted so far as Premier Bennett is concerned, started to trot off to Washington or some other country to deal directly with officials or agencies of that country, rather than such negotiations being carried on in the regular or recognized way.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to protest this government's surrender of its sovereign powers and its delegation of these powers to the government of British Columbia, particularly to Premier Bennett. I want to protest on behalf of this party this weak-kneed avoidance of responsibility in this most important matter. Finally, I say to the government: Stand up for Canada, represent Canada, and let us keep Canada a nation by so doing.

However, I think it ought to be raised, and some members ought to pay some attention to it. Originally, when the prime minister's residence was set up, at the insistence of the prime minister at that time, there was a provision that the prime minister would pay $5,000 a year for the privilege of living in the prime minister's residence. Naturally, the wishes of the prime minister at that time were respected. The fact is that this must impose a very serious burden on whoever is prime minister of Canada. I am told that the prime minister not only pays to live in the house but he must also hire his own chauffeur to drive his own car. I know he gets an allowance towards his car, but it would not begin to meet that kind of expense.
I am making the suggestion to the government that when they are drafting the estimates for next year, it seems to me that this ought to be re-examined. I think the time is overdue when we should take this item out of the legislative requirements and allow the prime minister to live in that house, as he ought to be allowed to do, without having to make any payments. Certainly, if he has, in addition, to hire a chauffeur and buy his own car, that is a burden. The prime minister cannot drive an ordinary car like the rest of us drive. He needs one that is commensurate with the dignity of the office

Approval of Expenditures, 1962-63 which he holds. Now, I do not believe hon. members want to impose that kind of burden upon any prime minister of this country. I should like to say, and I am sure most members of the house would agree, that if the government when they are bringing down their estimates for the next fiscal year, eliminated this $5,000 requirement and made some provision for supplying a chauffeur, that would meet with general approval.
