subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, July 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lamon-tagne for the second reading of Bill No. C-72,
Economic Council of Canada to provide tor the establishment of an economic council of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to talk about what this economic council is to do and what its chief purposes are. I shall do this in a fairly general way because I realize that there will be a closer discussion in the committee stage on the clauses of the bill. I shall focus my attention primarily on the first two of the three purposes which were outlined on Thursday last by the President of the Privy Council. The first purpose is that of economic research, forecasting and planning. The second is making policy recommendations on the basis of this research, forecasting and planning. The third purpose is to take over the functions of the national productivity council, which I believe is pretty well understood. In any event this will no doubt be discussed by others, so as I say, I shall restrict myself to the first two of the council's functions. In the course of doing this I should like to compare the role of the council, to some extent at any rate, with the proposed national economic development board introduced by the Conservative government in the last session.
The first duty of the council is to initiate and conduct basic research on all aspects of our economic life, and in particular to assess fairly regularly the medium term and long term prospects of the economy, and to compare such prospects with the potentialities of growth of the economy. It is also to study how economic growth, technological change and automation and international economic change may affect employment and incomes in Canada as a whole, in particular areas of Canada and in particular sectors of the economy, as well as the study of several other matters which are explicitly set out in the bill. These areas of study and research are set out more specifically in this bill, incidentally, than they were in the national economic development board bill introduced last session, and they are much more comprehensive. It seems to me, therefore, that the advice and recommendations which arise out of this basic research will be much more valuable. This is, then, the first distinction to which I would draw hon. members' attention between this bill and the one introduced in the last session.
I should think there is nothing very controversial about this provision for the collecting, co-ordinating and analysing of basic economic data. The only wonder is that it was not done years ago on a systematic and comprehensive basis. Actually, work of this kind was done during the latter war and early post-war years, particularly, it will be recalled, under the auspices of the department of reconstruction. Much of this work culminated in the federal government's well
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

known green book proposals. But as the boom of the mid and late forties came upon us, it seems to me that there was less inclination to probe into the problems and prospects of our economy, and I suppose this was natural enough. After all, why probe when it looks as though everything is going pretty well?
However, by the mid fifties concern was again shown about the prospects of the economy and some of its basic problems, and this led to the appointment of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects and the very valuable studies which it conducted. In the years that followed, despite the host of acute economic problems that arose, many of which had been foreseen in the Gordon report, the government of the day, it seems to me, showed little inclination for the kind of continuing economic research and analysis on a systematic and comprehensive basis which seemed, to this party at any rate, to be urgently required. A certain amount of basic, fundamental research has for some years now, it is true, been conducted in a few of our departments of government. For example, in the economics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce shortterm economic forecasting is carried on. But as the Glassco commission points out, the basic research which has been done in recent years has hardly been sufficient to build up adequate or profound knowledge of our economy.
There are various ways of getting more basic research done. For example, you could have a series of royal commissions. This is what Sweden used to do for its basic economic analysis and forecasting. I believe there was a commission for every period for which there was to be a plan. This has since been abandoned; but that is one way in which it could be done. Or you could try to have more basic research and analysis done in the various departments of government most concerned; or you could have a single research unit located in one department, possibly the Department of Finance.
I think, however, that the proposal for an economic council is best partly because it has other functions to perform apart from basic economic research. Even in the field of basic economic research I think it is the best kind of organizational set-up we could have. There is a tendency to let the economists who are employed in the various departments of government do the basic research last. It is regarded as something of a luxury, though it should not be. This is not at all likely to be the case in relation to special economic agencies. Furthermore, I think we are likely to get a sympathetic approach from the

senior people on the council, as it is constituted with the idea that research should be conducted on a systematic and continuing basis. Their attitude might be more sympathetic than in particular departments of government which are preoccupied from day to day with their own problems and with the carrying out of policy.
Much will undoubtedly depend, as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said, on the calibre of the chairman and of the full time members of the council. I think it is extremely important that these should be highly qualified persons with a great deal of knowledge in this field.
There is another reason why the council is a good idea, and this leads me to the second part of its first duty, namely, on the basis of its economic analysis and forecasts, the drawing up of an economic plan or plans. The economic council will be able to draw substantially both in its forecasting and in its planning on the resources of various parts of the economy. It will undoubtedly second economists from various departments of government. It will, I should think, second for short periods of time economists and others from private industry, from universities, from labour and elsewhere. I hope it will. It will also engage through its membership and through the standing committees which it is authorized to set up, in close collaboration with the public as well as the private sectors of the economy. I think it is implied in this bill that there will be very close consultation indeed between the council and its staff on one hand and the private sector of the economy on the other, as there will be between the council on the one hand and the agencies of the federal and provincial governments on the other. Indeed, the reliability of the forecasting and the usefulness of the planning will depend very much on the confidence established between government, labour, industry, provincial economic councils and so on. Therefore, there must be co-operation at this level.
In approaching the second phase of its first function, the council will, then, through its own membership, through the expert staff it employs, through the economists and others it seconds, as well as through the consultation it carries on with the other sectors of the economy both in the private and the public sectors, be able to gather up and attempt to co-ordinate the sum total of the plans and decisions of private and public bodies.
Here, it seems to me, is another major difference between this bill and the bill which was presented last year. There was nothing in that bill to suggest any kind of collaboration with either the private sector of the
Economic Council of Canada economy, or the public sector, including the provincial governments. The latter is all the more surprising because of the interest the party which was then in power professed to take in federal-provincial relations. But it seems to me they were taking a view of these relations which is, basically the watertight compartment view enunciated many years ago by the judicial committee, a view which has now resulted in the theory of federalism that I call the collision theory, namely that the federal government and the provincial governments shall each go their own chosen ways until one comes in contact with the other, until there is collision. In some areas it may be possible to carry on in this way, but in many areas of policy, particularly in those of public investment, I think we must revise our thinking about this entirely. We can no longer take a narrow, juristic point of view about this. It seems to me that where one has the federal government, provincial governments and municipalities together controlling about 30 per cent of all investment, and where, of that amount, the provinces and the municipalities actually have more economic weight than the federal government, there must be at a very early stage, as provided by this bill, some degree of discussion, some comparison of plans and intentions, some attempt at co-ordination. This is, in some respects, almost a revolutionary concept. Nevertheless, it is one which is being adopted now by some extremely able people, particularly in the provinces. I am thinking of Quebec and Saskatchewan where I have heard this view frequently expressed, but it is current in others, too.
Therefore, an important element of this bill is the provision it makes in the last paragraph of clause 9 for consultation of this kind, to some extent in forecasting but particularly in drawing up plans indicating desired levels of investment and other matters. Similarly it is important to have collaboration of this kind with the private sector of the economy and, again, the bill makes provision for this to be done. Taking the field of investment again, the remaining 70 per cent of investment in this country, as is well known, is largely in the hands of three or four dozen large corporations. These, in recent years, have, in a way, been far more progressive than the government in realizing that there must be much more involvement with the public sector than was the case in the past, more need for planning. Therefore there is this important provision that the council study and discuss with the various elements in the private sector what specific plans for production and investment in major industries in Canada will best contribute to a high and consistent rate of economic growth. The
2208	HOUSE OF
Economic Council of Canada economic council will not be a body of pure researchers totally removed from everyday life, and it seems to me it is important to point this out. The other members of the council, the people who are drawn from various representative organizations, will, of course, keep in touch with broad movements, attitudes and ideas in Canadian society. As I say, the staff of the council itself will be composed not only of a body of permanent people but will be drawn from various parts of both the public and private sectors; and I should think that the council will engage in fairly continuous consultation with the major elements that have the main weight in our economic life.
As a result of this research and consultation the council, as I have suggested, draws up an economic plan or plans. The fact that it should draw up a plan at all, the fact that it should say, after its investigation to see what the growth potentialities of the economy are, here is a target rate of growth or a feasible rate of growth and we will now work out in detail by economic sectors and regions the amounts of investment that the achievement of this rate of growth requires, is a major departure. The fact that it does this also makes the present bill different from that of last session. On the basis of its economic analysis and forecasts, its consultation, its attempt to try to get together all the help it can, the council will inevitably spell out the implications, in investment and in other fields, for individual industries, especially the major industries, and I should think also the implications for the various public sectors of the economy.
I have been using the illustration of investment but one can use others equally well. The bill envisages, as I say, close collaboration between the public and private sectors of the economy both in economic forecasting and in drawing up the kind of economic plan that will or might make the target rate of growth attainable. The council in itself, according to the bill, does not have the power actually to implement its plan or plans. It cannot say to industry: All right, we have examined the investment picture with you and you are to conform with our investment program, with what we think is the ideal amount of investment for you to be engaging in over such and such a period of time. It does not have any coercive power. Indeed, I know very few planning agencies in the democratic world which have coercive power. It is really almost a red herring to suggest that they do.
What power does the council have? First of all, it has the power of publicizing its views, of publicizing its plan. Here we come to another difference between this bill and


the one last year, in that the council will not only initiate studies, which is extremely important in itself, but will publish an annual review of economic prospects and problems which will undoubtedly improve public understanding and certainly will raise the level of public discussion. I think there might be even further areas of publication possible for this council.
I agree with the leader of the Social Credit party who argued on Thursday the importance of publishing as much as possible. I have already pointed out one great improvement over last year's bill in this connection and there may be others. Certainly from the standpoint of educational value, for persuading businessmen to take a longer term view of growth, for educating government at all levels, and the public, in the policies required to facilitate growth and educating them generally as to other objectives, there is perhaps nothing so important as publication.
The council will also have the power of recommendation, and we come to its second major duty or function. It will have the power to recommend policies to the federal government that will contribute to bringing our economic prospects more closely in line with our potentialities of growth, to recommend policies that will in effect implement the plan that has been drawn up. There is no reason that some of these recommendations, where they fall in areas outside the jurisdiction of the federal government, cannot be made available to private industry, the provincial sector, municipalities and so on. In some cases I should think this would be possible, and certainly it is desirable.
In other words, this is the very opposite of planning for planning's sake, which was one of the arguments the official opposition put forward the other day. You would have planning for planning's sake if you did not do anything, if you simply had a bunch of people sitting around drawing up lovely plans, and that was that. What you have here is the hope that the plan may be implemented. There is no coercive power. There is a persuasive power. If the membership of the council is drawn from highly qualified people there is no doubt it will have quite a strong persuasive power. And it does have the power -I agree this was also in the Conservative bill of last year but it was so hidden I had a difficult time finding it-to make recommendations for the kind of government policies that will best implement the plan. These may be recommendations that involve a kind of intervention that we do not now have. They may be recommendations that involve only the implementation of the kinds of

policies we have had in the past, fiscal, tariff, tax, monetary and other policies.
The bill in itself naturally does not say what kind of policies might be recommended. For all one knows, the policies recommended might actually involve less intervention in toto by government rather than more. I was reading a book the other day which many hon. members have read recently, "Beyond the Welfare State" by Gunnar Myrdal. By the way, I hope it is still not too un-Canadian to read books, as it apparently is to write them. If I may digress for a moment, may I say I was shocked by the remark of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) last Thursday that "the last thing a person going into politics should do is write a book". I must confess that as I listened to that remark it seemed to me it would exclude from politics, Winston Churchill, Harold Wilson, President Kennedy, Prime Minister Nehru, President Radhakrishnan, President de Gaulle. Indeed, as I ran down the list I realized it would exclude everybody but the right hon. gentleman. Actually I mean this quite seriously. I am shocked at a statement like that. It may be, of course, that he was scourging the party to which I belong because some of its members have written books. Perhaps he did not intend the statement the way it came across, but what came across so strongly to me, and I am sure to other members of the house, was that he meant what be said-that the last thing one should do if one is going into politics is to write a book.

speechtext: Or even read one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Just do not let the halls of parliament become halls of learning; perish the thought. I do hope that there were no young people in the galleries to hear this kind of advice. In any event, as I say, I hope it is not contrary to the Canadian way of life either to write books or to read books.
After this small digression I should like to return to the book "Beyond the Welfare State", by Gunnar Myrdal who says that planning is probably the only alternative to the chaos created by unco-ordinated and disorganized state intervention, the very kind of unco-ordinated, disorganized, ad hoc intervention we have known in this country for too long, and especially during the last few years. Rather than being the bureaucratic confusion which the Leader of the Opposition described, it could well result in the very opposite, the more rational use of the power of the state which I am sure is something we all really want in the long run.
Finally, whether the government will adopt policies that are recommended, whether it
Economic Council of Canada will try to implement, so far as it has jurisdiction to do so, the plans that are drawn up, will depend of course entirely upon the government. Whether it will use the old tools or whether it will fashion new tools, will also depend a great deal on the government of the day, upon the conditions of the day, upon the attitudes and state of mind of the Canadian public. I would think it quite possible, after this council has been in existence for a while, that the Canadian public will become much more aware and knowledgeable of the Canadian economy, its problems and prospects. We might then become much more willing to use what I call a rational use of the state in areas where we can aid and increase employment, make for a better rate of economic growth and provide a better life for Canadians.
What is clear is that whatever action the government takes, it will undoubtedly be positive action. It may hurt some sectors of the economy. Whatever action the government takes will be on the basis, first, of more fundamental research than heretofore and, secondly, on a more integrated approach. It will function on the basis of a much greater degree of consultation with the public sector, federal, provincial and municipal, and with the private sector. Third, whatever action the government takes will be on the basis of a plan or a model. The philosophy underlining this government's approach is, I think, undoubtedly that of Robert Marjolin who said in the European economic commission's report put out in Brussels in 1962:
Doubtless it is possible to make good policy without planning if the needs are so evident that there could be no doubt as to what action to take. Where they are not so evident a great deal of information and thought may be needed. In the present circumstances of very considerable uncertainty, of rapidly changing conditions, planning can help to make a rational economic policy possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the last speaker is concerned, I wish to state how pleasant it was to listen to her. If the new board that is being envisaged by this measure has few persuasive powers, I am sure the hon. lady has many persuasive powers. I should like her to use them to try to persuade her government to do the things that will accomplish some of the objectives she has mentioned, instead of simply talking about them and further confusing an already confused situation as a result of events which have taken place since April 21 last. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, this evening I should like to focus my remarks on the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) to whom I
listened with great interest and respect the
2210	HOUSE OF
Economic Council of Canada other evening. He talked with that certain confidence-that I could describe as doctrinal-for which he is known in his pronun-tiamento ex cathedra to which he has become accustomed for some time now. He also indulged in most interesting economic prophecies, theoretically of course, and I congratulate him for that.
He took the liberty of scrutinizing the mysteries of economic cycles and I would readily recognize that no one is as qualified as he is to do so. And in the course of his scrutiny he happened to make some discoveries. He stated that among other things our Canadian economy was suffering from a stagnant condition, I even believe that he used the phrase "chronic anemia".
Furthermore, I found that, in 1954, when he was writing his book on Canadian federalism, which has been abundantly commented on in this house during this debate and preceding ones, he made precisely the same remarks we have just heard, as shown on page 136 of his book, which contains some statements about the economic stagnation found in several parts of the world, particularly in Canada. In fact, he stated-and he was perfectly right to do so:
The nightmare of economic depressions, during which production falls sharply, has surely not vanished yet. Finally, practically nothing has been done to put a stop to seasonal declines in production. Far from having been overcome, those difficulties are still the greatest economic problems we will have to tackle.
A little further he said:
That is why the government policy must aim first at assuring a balanced expansion or, more exactly, a national revenue and an employment level that will be stable and high.
He was right in saying that and I congratulate him for doing so at that time, by taking an entirely non-partisan stand. However, in his remarks last Thursday, the President of the Privy Council seemed to believe that that economic anemia had developed during these last few years, although in 1954, when his party was at the peak of its political history, we were faced with the same problem.
Dealing with the causes of that chronic stagnation the minister said, as stated on page 2086 of Hansard for July 11, 1963:
-our private sector has almost exhausted the investment potentialities which technology created in Canada at the beginning of this century.
Obviously, the minister who is an expert in economic matters, had no intention of allowing us into the inner circle of those policies. He told the members that he was
[Mr. Martineau.l

sparing them the details and in doing so he took, in a way, a take-it-or-leave-it attitude.
Indeed, I did not expect that he would waste that valuable science in dispensing it to laymen or to run-of-the-mill members of parliament.
In concluding, the minister said that the private sector left to itself cannot overcome those difficulties. Speaking of economic stagnation he said that we need a bolder and more dynamic government leadership, in other words a plan so that the various aspects of the economic policy will be well co-ordinated and so that the private sector can work hand in hand with the government.
He is against imperative planning for Canada because in his opinion, it would be politically unacceptable, economically undesirable and constitutionally unworkable. I entirely agree with the minister in that respect. But when he speaks about things that are politically unacceptable, economically undesirable, and constitutionally unworkable, has he stopped to think that it is precisely those things that the government to which he belongs has been offering us for the past few weeks?
As far as politically unacceptable things are concerned, could you find anything more so-and I merely point this out as an example-than some of the taxes applied by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in his recent budget? As a matter of fact, those taxes were economically disastrous and politically unacceptable to such an extent that the minister had to beat a retreat. I am convinced, besides, that if it had been possible to save face at the same time, his retreat would have been complete.
Let us now deal with those things that are constitutionally unworkable.
In the first place, let us consider the statements made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech on the priority requirements of central authorities in fiscal matters. Let us consider the municipal development and loan bill. Let us consider the establishment of the department of industry. Let us consider some of the statements made by his colleagues in this house indicating that the government is prompted by a spirit of centralization such as has never been witnessed before in the history of Canadian confederation.
He mentioned later that the planning advocated by the government and which it intends to establish in Canada is essentially a form of planning which shows the way and provides incentives-in other words that it is an indicative planning similar to the French pattern.

Near the end of his speech, he said that the bill provides for the establishment of an economic council with very extensive powers which would give planning a scope that would be comprehensive as well as flexible. Then he added that the legislation was of primary importance.
In short, he is only restating the theories put forward in his book "Canadian federalism" which, in order to be implemented, would require a new centralizing offensive.
Besides, the minister had expressed his inner convictions on that connection in his book, which is entirely imbued, if I am not mistaken, with centralizing motives and where that idea is found, among other things, on page 282. I shall quote a few sentences:
Finally, a program of economic stability requiring a central direction and a well-integrated economic policy. All those factors indicate that the federal government will have to play a major role-
Those are the important words-
-a major role in the collective fight against instability. The insistence put on the finer aspects of country life-
-says the minister-
-has not solved the problems created by migration towards the cities.
That is a good example but it could be slightly changed to read as follows: The insistence put on the advantages of provincial autonomy will not solve the economic problems of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the minister seems to think that I have great imagination but I must say that my statement is truly in the spirit of his remarks.
The minister wishes this country to adopt methods of planning which surely would not be workable within our federative framework.
On the other hand, we must ask ourselves if the object of the bill we are studying, and which aims at the creation of a Canadian economic council, is truly the establishment of economic planning in this country. The minister himself has said that such was the object of the bill.
Again, are we sure that the planning spoken about by the government is, in fact, what is called directive and indicative planning, similar to the indicative planning we find in France?
Mr. Speaker, there is not the slightest adumbration of planning in this bill. Let us take a good look at it.
One only has to read certain provisions of this bill to find many harmless words like 28902-5-141
Economic Council of Canada study, examine, analyse, compare and recommend.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that we are among a group of normal school students. This is mere window dressing. Even though we consider all the scope, all the powers of the bill, this does not even constitute a starting point to the establishment of a planned system in Canada.
The minister may say: Well, those are partly the terms used to introduce the bill in the house last year. It is true, it has been largely copied, but at least, when the government of the time proposed the bill last year, they did not endeavour to tell us that, by that measure, they were creating some sort of planning in Canada. They merely said that the purpose of the project was to give our economy a sense of direction and to the government the benefit of experts in such matters who were available in Canada.
Consider section 9, Mr. Speaker, which is as follows:
It shall be the duty of the council to advise and recommend to the minister-
To advise and recommend, those are the general duties of the council. To advise and recommend. Then the bill leaves the general for the particular and says that the council will have the responsibility "regularly to assess"-what does that mean? And we also read that the council's duties will be:
To recommend government policies-
To consider means-
To study means of increasing Canadian participation in ownership, to study implications, to study and discuss with representatives of the industries concerned and with representatives of labour, farmers,-
Cliches, nothing but cliches.
To study how national economic policies can best foster the balanced economic development of all areas of Canada.
To explore and evaluate particular projects of major significance for the expansion of industrial activities-
To encourage maximum consultation and cooperation between labour and management-
To seek full and regular consultation with appropriate agencies of the governments of the several provinces.
To encourage, promote, organize and so forth.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I challenge the minister to prove how, with all those recommendations, with all those studies, all those analyses and all those comparisons, we will get this capital project he talks about, as well as a planned economy in Canada.

Economic Council of Canada
Mr. Speaker, if we look at French planning, we realize that it is a very different story. First, in French planning, practice came before theory. Here it is the theoretical planning of the minister which comes first. We find loud theories which help cover the lack of substance. If Montaigne were here, he would certainly wonder where is in all that the substantial marrow. Where is the substance towards which all energies will concentrate to establish planning, a guiding policy?

speechtext:
There is nothing in all that, as I said earlier. A while ago, I was telling the minister that we had not tried to put in that project something which was not to be found in it. But here, Mr. Speaker, it is just the opposite. Here we really have the mountain that brings forth a mouse and nothing else.
In France, planning constitutes a collective work aimed at a co-ordinated economy and, to use the words of the French lecturer Pierre Masse, it is not a concert of chamber music but a symphony requiring several thousand performers.
The French planning commission is made up of some 150 experts, but with its 25 renovation boards and 20 economic and social operational groups, there are about 3,500 people.
But in this case, Mr. Speaker, I put it to you that this project will give us no plan nor even a commission. And the minister rises at his place in the house and tells us most emphatically that we have before us a major contribution, the beginning of planning.
No, these are empty words, pompous remarks, because if we go beyond the surface, looking for the contents of this bill, we find absolutely nothing. We are misleading the Canadian people if we imply that we have in it indicative planning along the line of the French pattern.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider the French plan, we see that it bears on energy producing industries, such as coal, electrical power, steel, and transportation. The emphasis is put on a reduction of prices and an organization of markets, scientific and technical development together with a specialization of enterprise.
Now, Mr. Speaker, those things can be accomplished in a country like France which

has a unified government, but I submit that they cannot be accomplished under our federal system, particularly without prior consultation with the provinces. The minister was very careful not to mention that he had had any consultation with the provincial governments in that regard before submitting this legislation with such a fanfare.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the French plan is a logical one with a Cartesian outlook. It tends to economic integration in transferring to the national level the techniques of business agreements of private law.
Here again we are in a field strictly reserved to the provinces, the field of civil law, private law. That is why planning such as the minister wants to force upon us, is not at all feasible under the present system.
Mr. Speaker, this same French plan has a great number of modernization boards, vertical and horizontal boards, and so on. The formulation of the plan implies a strong centralization and very extensive powers for the federal government.
I know that such a centralization of powers is quite acceptable in the opinion of the minister, but it is not acceptable to a great number of members of the house and especially to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, in the preparation of the French plan, a great many commissions set up first preliminary drafts respecting production, employment, investments and decide upon a desirable rate of growth. Then, those drafts are submitted to the government which selects a desirable rate of growth.
The government itself consults the investment section as well as the economic and social council.
Now, those organizations do not exist under our system and their establishment is not foreseen in this project or in any other legislative program now before us.
The government having made its choice, the modernization boards prepare a first preliminary synthesis and then a meeting is held between experts and members of the planning board who, after discussion and settlement of contentious points, agree to prepare a final synthesis with regard to the implementation of the plan. That plan is submitted to the government, discussed in the chamber of deputies and then approved by the president of the council. Afterward, that plan becomes the official plan for the next four or five years in France.

It should be noted in all this that the French government holds greater implementation powers than the Canadian government; besides the minister said that it was much better that way, under our system.
Besides, in France, the government sets up its budget policy according to the development program thus drafted. Here we did not do that in this case. The last budget did not have any planning implications, Mr. Speaker; it was rather the opposite.
The government sets up its credit and fiscal policies according to the objectives of the plan. Besides, in France, the government has a direct control over almost half the investments. Here in Canada, I think it is 15 per cent. So we realize that the two systems have nothing in common.
Also, in France, the government may resort to incentives, such as fiscal incentives, the granting of credit priorities and the advantages given companies which meet the objectives of the plan.
If all that is not direct coercion, it is at least an indirect form of coercion. I have noticed no indication yet that the government would be prepared to impose that form of coercion and give the country these means of implementing a real program of indicative planning.
There is absolutely no adumbration of planning in this bill or in the others submitted to the house. On the contrary, I believe that the legislation that has been introduced constitutes a confused heap of divergent interests who were anxious to be heard.
In a pretence of action, the government decided to take some measures without asking itself whether those measures were meeting actual needs of the country.
I am convinced that the measures proposed by the government are not likely to put an end to this stagnation, this chronic anemia, which the minister mentioned last Thursday. Quite clearly, Mr. Speaker, this bill does not make for economic planning in this country. If the minister is sincere-and I believe he does genuinely wish to improve economic, cultural and social conditions in Canada- I suggest that he advise his colleagues, and more particularly the Prime Minister, to call immediately, to start with, a dominion-provincial conference, and not only a conference such as the Prime Minister announced today, regarding municipalities and the contributory 28902-5-141J
Economic Council of Canada pension scheme, but a dominion-provincial conference to deal specifically and exclusively with economic problems.
Then, too, let the government set up permanent federal-provincial co-operative agencies, possibly a secretariat to deal with economic matters.
I think it is of first importance that the plans prepared by the government be thus established in the light of historical circumstances and constitutional needs. Let us define correctly the economic duties at both levels of government so that there will be no duplication of efforts and especially no conflicts of interests and jurisdiction.
Since this government has been in power conflicts have grown in numbers; new conflicts of authority have risen incessantly to such an extent that-and I do not think I am wrong in saying this-never have dominion-provincial relations been in such a pitiful state as they are since this government came to power. And, for pity's sake, let us forget about the concept of the leading position of the federal state.
In his book, in which he refers to the so-called advantageous position of the federal government, the minister states repeatedly that the provinces do not have the proper financial means and taxation power to implement those plans. Only if the balance is restored between the central government and the province in the field of taxation, in accordance with the provisions of the constitution, will provincial governments be able to play their true role.
Thus we would create the proper climate to stimulate the economy of the country instead of making relations worse.
In addition, the proposed consultations should be more than the reflex of politicians who find themselves in the wrong. When we were considering the bill for the establishment of a department of industry, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Drury) stated that neither he nor the government had to consult the provinces in that connection. According to him, the members of the government are fully aware of the dividing line between federal and provincial jurisdiction and there is no call for a federal-provincial conference in that respect.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I submit that it is precisely this arrogant attitude, this way of deciding by oneself what others must do that has given rise to ill feeling. I challenge the minister and his colleagues to deny that the climate has taken a sharp turn for the worse

Economic Council of Canada in the past tew weeks. It is obvious and the facts are there to prove it.
Mr. Speaker, if we were to proceed in the manner I have just outlined I believe we could set up an intelligent and co-ordinated economic policy which would involve the kind of planning we need today-as no one will deny-and which would truly meet the needs of all our people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened with great interest to the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) who obviously tried to find some meat in the statements of the Liberal party. However, if the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue finds that federal-provincial relations are now somewhat down to earth, there is an explanation to this: the government which I support is an active government. We take measures and we draft a policy which is of course facing some opposition. But unlike the previous government, we, on this side of the house, are doing things.
The problems between the federal government and the provinces will be solved by negotiations. The present Prime Minister took steps to solve those problems. We, as members of the federal government, have no right to stay inactive on that account. We have to take action and we do take action, something that our friends, the Conservatives, failed to do in previous years.
The hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue is concerned about the meaning of the bill before us, but if he would analyse its provisions, he would realize that we also want planning, a kind of planning that entails action. The economic council will be an economic planning council that will succeed. We will have the necessary staff provided by this piece of legislation that will give the federal government the possibility of providing for the future; something which has never been envisaged by our friends opposite and the lack of which has put the country in its present position.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is concerned about the fact that the government has perhaps called in experts to discuss the matter with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne). Let him be assured that I am not an expert, only a backbencher, but that I have faith in the planning policy of the party which I support.

I think that Bill C-72 which provides for the establishment of an economic council of Canada is very important and I hope that all hon. members of the house will give it the importance it deserves. Administration in Canada is so much more difficult because the country is a kind of a geographic nonsense in a political unit. The fact that citizens of Victoria in British Columbia, of Halifax in Nova Scotia and of St. John's in Newfoundland are all grouped under the same legislative authority, while there is a whole continent between them and that on this vast territory the density of population is relatively small, that is the reason why our country attained the various stages of economic growth later than our most immediate friends, Great Britain, France and the United States.
According to Professor W. W. Rostow of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in his book entitled The Stages of Economic Growth, Canada attained in 1950 the same degree of economic maturity, as regards technology, close to 50 years after the above-mentioned countries. Why? Because Canada just about came out of the preparation period to enter the technological development period which could bring our country to an economic maturity. In fact, to date, we have used our energies for the development of our natural resources in this raw state and the setting up of basic public services such as railways and great road projects. In other words, it is only in the last few years that our country has been in a position to carry out the development of an economy more diversified and more able to meet the needs of a labour force more and more specialized and numerous.
In that context, I think the development of our economy is in a very critical situation today and I sincerely think that we must go ahead with economic planning in our country.
The present situation calls for an immediate positive action to make known to the nation the precise objectives which our economy must reach.
We must without delay direct the development of our economy according to our possibilities, our natural resources, our increasing manpower and our international markets. Finally, every person will have to do his utmost to achieve the aims determined by the economic council and devote all his energies to that end.

However, the country will not achieve those aims without an appropriate intervention from the state. The federal government will have to legislate in the fields coming under its jurisdiction and devolved to it by the constitution, such as credit, taxation, tariffs, in a co-ordinate and positive way, so that the aims sought might be achieved in the shortest possible time and that the public and private enterprises are not left alone to seek those aims. All those potential supplies of natural wealth available to Canada must be developed in a rational way, so that the Canadian people may derive the greatest possible profit to which they are entitled. But in order to achieve this, our government must adopt positive and effective policies, even though private enterprise must be ready to make certain sacrifices.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to refer to the province of Quebec as an example. During the past few years, it has launched economic development projects and has completely nationalized its water resources to achieve one of its economic purposes. It is now getting ready, through a joint public and private body, the "Societe generale de Financement", to develop a large steel complex. I think that it is an example that we should take into consideration and try to follow, if necessary.
I am definitely in favour of indicative but not of imperative planning. But the necessary means should be made available to us in order that the purposes which will be put forward by the future economic council be achieved without delay even if they are detrimental to a few.
In fact, nobody likes going to the dentist to have a tooth taken out but it is a temporary pain for a future good.
I want to point out two particular points of Bill C-72. The first one concerns the appointment of three permanent directors for a seven year term. In my opinion, the appointments of those three directors will have to be considered very seriously and carefully. I think the council formed of those three permanent directors will be in a position, under the provisions of this bill, to carry out very serious and thorough studies on the Canadian economy. And this work will have to be done speedily and result without delay in precise aims for the country.
Consequently, I feel we must give a much greater importance to this triumvirate than to the 25 non-permanent members of the council. This 25 member council may inform the permanent council of the people's views,
Economic Council of Canada and the latter will immediately have to set about supplying us with the necessary plan to lead our economy where we want it to go.
At this stage, I would like to say that I found very interesting the suggestions of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), who, incidentally, approves the principle of this legislation and would like those three permanent directors to be appointed for the government's lifetime, that is not for a set period of seven, eight, nine or ten years, but for the duration of the government. He states that this course is followed in the United States, with interesting results. I refer to the necessity for consultation with the provincial governments. Just as much progress has been made at the provincial government level as has been made by the federal government to meet the new demands of government in our complex twentieth century society. Indeed, many of the problems with which the council is designed to deal actually come under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. This is an area where extreme care will have to be used if we are to realize the positive effects which can be achieved by a council of this kind. I am sure I do not have to admonish the government in this respect, because they have already felt the strength of the negative response that can occur in this delicate federal-provincial balance of power when the central government neglects to consult with the provincial governments concerning matters that are of extreme importance and concern to these governments.
During the resolution stage of the debate I referred to this point in passing, pointing out that the province of Manitoba, as an example of one province, is away ahead of Ottawa in dealing with the economic challenges of the new kind of economy in which we live. Most hon. members will have received recently this voluminous report from the government of Manitoba entitled "Manitoba 1962-1975", which indicates that here is a province that is away out ahead of the federal government. Manitoba has a Conservative government which drew its inspiration from the leadership provided by the former federal Conservative government. I trust that the minister responsible will be guided by the very excellent analysis of contemporary economic problems provided in this report. It covers every segment of the economy and I feel is an excellent reminder at this critical juncture in Canadian affairs that the provinces have their own important

sphere of influence, and any undue interference on the part of the national government is not going to be too helpful in continuing the high level of economic activity that was achieved by the former administration.
This is a federal state, and one must always remember that relationships among senior governments are delicate because of the very nature of confederation. Much of the Canadian economy belongs to the provinces. The resources belong to the provinces. The provinces, therefore, are not going to countenance any undue intrusion by Ottawa, particularly without prior consultation and certainly without concern for their sensitivities and prerogatives in this regard.
I should also like to suggest that the private sector, or the voluntary sector of the Canadian economy is most important in this respect. This report was prepared entirely by a committee of volunteers, none of whom received any stipend from the provincial government. I am afraid that sometimes governments of all stripes tend to feel they are responsible for everything that takes place in the economy. Of course, that is the authoritarian point of view, and in a democratic society one must always realize that in the final analysis it is the creativity of the people of the country, their spirit of co-operation, their initiative which will determine whether the economy continues to prosper.
In a council of this kind let us make the utmost use of the advice, services and initiative in the private sector of the economy. The private initiative is of basic importance. In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, I trust that hon. members of the house, and particularly the members of the government, will agree that the best contribution a government can make in the field of economic development and economic health is to provide the atmosphere and climate in which the ordinary citizen, whether he be a businessman, a member of the labouring community, a farmer, or whatever his calling, can exert his maximum influence. It is the climate, the atmosphere, that matters.
I trust the climate that has been established-as has been pointed out so eloquently in this unbiased, objective report from the economists of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce-will continue to thrive; that the example set by the previous administration will be duly noted by the new administration so they will forget their propaganda and deal with positive policies.

former government. We like to believe that there are improvements. We hope there are. We think that the duties of the council as set out in clause 9 are much more specific. I hope that will not happen.
I hope that in making the appointments there will be a genuine attempt to ensure that they shall be representative, and I hope also representative of some of the best academic opinion. It is about time that we recognized those people who are trained in economics and who know something about general interests as distinct from private and special interests. We must have representatives of people in business who are prepared to take risks and think in the largest and broadest way. If we look at the situation in Britain, the Neddy committee presided over by Reginald Maudling, we can see that it is possible to have big men on this kind of council, men whose special interests to some extent cancel one another out and who are prepared to reach some sort of economic consensus.
We have not been able to articulate and enunciate adequately the consensus that I think most of us in this country share. Personally I was very disappointed in the budget debate. It was more preoccupied with personalities than with policy. But we seem all agreed so far as the grievous imbalance in our trade situation is concerned. We are concerned

We are concerned, I think, that so much of our agricultural market is now directed to a certain group of communist countries and that we have lost that diversification of market which in the past we enjoyed.
I do not think we can actually blame the Conservative administration for these changes. Let us collectively face these problems fairly and factually. Personally I feel that the fact that there is a minority government at the moment offers perhaps the most hopeful possibility of Canada reaching some kind of new consensus on economic matters.
The United States has had some experience with its employment act of 1946. I know there are people in the New Democratic party who feel that this was a very faltering, stumbling and hesitant step. Perhaps the achievements of that group in the United States would not satisfy the distinguished member from Northumberland. But the Americans have had a great tradition of reliance on the private sector and it was in the private sector particularly that they found they needed a council of economic advisers. Why? To prevent depressions, to maintain a high level of employment-although heaven knows it has not been high enough-to bolster production and purchasing power. The objective of their council of economic advisers was to place the economic development of their country under continuous scrutiny, to make policy recommendations to the president and to give the United States the ability to look ahead, or what I have referred to as "prevoyance".
We want research and analysis, the determination of objectives, the discovery of alternative solutions, the formulation of policies, the execution of a plan. This council cannot do anything, of course, except indicate; but it is very important to indicate, and when the appointments are made by the government I hope that a great deal of emphasis will be placed on the chairman and the two other permanent members of the council.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who made an excellent speech on this subject. It seems to me that we will be going places with this council if the permanent secretariat is strong and is made up of people of great ability and distinction, and with a certain amount of personal influence and power. If in making up the total board of 25 there are selected top ranking men from industry, labour, agriculture and so on, I believe that these men can sit down and face facts, perhaps more easily than we can ourselves. I think that already they are aware of many of the facts. I have had businessmen tell me that even if
Economic Council of Canada an industry has to face difficult times ahead it is better that it should know the facts. For example, if a sector of the textile industry has to face the prospect of going out of business because it is going to be replaced by something else that is more productive, it is far better that the industry should know what the future holds in order to move sensibly and wisely.
After all, today there is not the sharp cleavage between capital and labour that prevailed in the time of the early private entrepreneurial organizations. To my knowledge I do not know one person who really is a capitalist in the full sense of the word. The people who run the 10 to 12 industries in my home city are really labour people. They are a part of management. They are highly skilled and highly trained. Very few of them own very much in the way of stock, perhaps just a little by way of token ownership; but essentially they are not owners. They are management and they are trying to do a scientific and wise job. Therefore I emphasize the fact that if we are going to make the economic council of Canada vigorous and strong the most important thing is the appointments.
I have been somewhat concerned about the wording appearing in clause 4, subclause 2, which provides that each of the other members of the council shall be appointed after consultation with appropriate representative organizations, to hold office for a term of three years. I hope that when the government finally proceeds to make these appointments, if the bill is passed, they will look for top quality in each appointment; and that is not obtained simply by appointing the person who happens to be the president or secretary treasurer of a certain organization. When we look at the British appointments to Neddy I think we are satisfied there has been a certain amount of wisdom shown in the choice of those people who represent, for example, the rubber industry or the cotton industry. The man who represents, for instance, the academic community is a person highly advanced in the economics of labour a man head and shoulders over other people in his field. The representative of the national coal board happens to be the chairman. We have, of course, people in high positions representing unions, representing boards of trade and so on. In my opinion, the quality of these important appointments is of primary significance.
The danger is, of course, that with a large 25-man board, it may become a meeting society to talk, dine occasionally and move off in directions that really accomplish very little. I hope, like the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) that the permanent

Economic Council of Canada secretary, the chairman and his two permanent members, will be men of individual ability and talent, that they will work as a team and that we will have before us annually for consideration the kind of report which is in substance a little Gordon commission report. It is this kind of thing that I should like to see. Of course they may go off in various productive sidetracks. They can develop interests in special areas, and these will be necessary; but largely this is going to be a board that is thinking not in terms of tactics, the mechanics of production, but essentially in terms of economic strategy and projecting a plan for growth covering the next decade, two decades or perhaps even longer.
We know that there is going to be foreign investment in this country. We do not want to see ourselves cut off from capital. It seems to me that the great adventure of this particular decade for Canada will be the progressive steps taken by government to make us part of the new international community. We must preserve the general interest and become more objective. We must become more involved in every respect in foreign aid, in our involvement with other nations on this continent, in Europe and elsewhere. It seems to me that there will be a sharp shift from the kind of economic nationalism that has prevailed in this country pretty well since confederation, that is the significant change that is going to take place. I believe that this is in the long-run interest, not only of the maritimes, not only of the agricultural west, but even of the highly developed and industrialized areas of Quebec and Ontario. I believe that the areas in which we are going to make startling progress are those areas in which we can at last compete on a larger scale.
I hope sincerely, Mr. Speaker, that we can approach this new concept of planning, not in the sense of thinking that any small group of people are so much wiser than other people, but that Canadians must work progressively towards this new economic consensus, this new harmony, this larger cooperation between the productive elements. I look particularly for co-operation between the private and public sectors, as was stressed by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett). This is important. She stressed a fact of life in Canada, that approximately one third of our investment, about one third of our employment, is dependant upon the public sector. We are going to blind ourselves entirely to these important considerations if appointments to this council are directed only to the private sector.

On the other hand, I think the members of our group do believe that we must and can plan for increased competition, and that capitalism has virtue only if it is competitive. This is the thing for which we are striving. It is said that the first aim of a government is to create an atmosphere for economic growth. The first objective of any sensible economic system must be to increase the wealth of the community. One listens with some little concern to statements about the likelihood of our hurried implementation of certain social security programs when we really do not know how large an economic pie we are going to have to distribute. Personally, I am just a little old fashioned about this, and I look with anxiety on the fact that we are urged to spend before we know where this money is coming from. This is perhaps the result of a Presbyterian background; I don't know. It seems to me that if the economic council can help to bake the larger pie then, in our wisdom, we can attend to this necessary process of redistribution which finally brings justice to every element in the community.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, planning is one of the purposes of this legislation. Now, the purpose of economic activity has always been to increase production with the least possible efforts.
We are endeavouring to establish a temporal social order in which the human being could live normally to attain its complete fulfilment. Controlled planning which seeks to determine the right to production based solely on labour devoted to that end, becomes increasingly dangerous with the advance of applied science.
Such a result could be expected, as this is contrary to the natural order and takes a means for an end. Economics are intended to provide goods, and not to control or govern people. Labour is considered as a means to some extent, as far as it is necessary to reach an end.
To associate money, which is the right to production, solely with labour, is therefore to subordinate the end to the means. In short, it is more than a surrender, it is a shameful humiliation, inasmuch as modern progress increases the level of production.
To associate money solely with employment leads necessarily to state control with all its resulting perils and subservience.
Workers get paid to produce consumer goods; but since machines and men have

become inseparable, the price of those consumer goods far exceeds the money distributed to workers in return for their participation. Since the market is already flooded, very few are interested in setting up new factories in such conditions.
That is where the government is forced to intervene, but since it clings to old principles and it does not want to create debt free money, it has to take the money out of the pockets of the taxpayers, either through taxation or loans. Then, to save the principle of money based solely on labour, it has to employ people under the conditions of patronage which corrupts politics.
Here again, in a world of conflict, the production of cannons, machine-guns, planes, nuclear arms and means of destruction of all kinds becomes a magnificent introduction. Not only does the production of goods which are not for sale ensure the distribution of money, but it does not create the same problems as the production of ordinary capital goods, since there are no commodities to be sold.
On the contrary, if cannons, bombers and torpedoes are put to work, they destroy great quantities of all kinds of goods, and this greatly helps to reduce supply to the level of purchasing power and, at the same time, it paves the way for reconstruction which will keep a lot of people busy.
Since the aim of economics is employment, war is a godsend for civilized countries where automation throws so many people out of work.
That is why we claim that to base money solely on work is to call for excessive intervention by the state with all the disorders that such an intervention entails. It is also for that reason that war is the ideal means of restoring the balance between the products on the shelves and the money in the consumer's pockets. In fact, the more machinery you have-under present regulations-the closer you are to war, which increases the amount of money in circulation while it cuts down on surplus goods and labour.
A more humane way to get out of this situation would be through a social dividend, by creating money to increase purchasing power directly and to bring it to the same level as the supply of consumer goods. Thus, instead of fostering war, machinery would justify the payment of a dividend to every member of society.
That is also why we say that if socialist countries had applied Social Credit, they would have brought about in the world,
Economic Council of Canada through the example of the larger countries, an economy of peaceful prosperity, and mankind would have considered them as geniuses and honoured them as great benefactors. But the Social Credit dividend is not on better terms with the Marxist or the Bolshevist philosophy than it is with that of the banker.
Dictators, in Berlin or Moscow, like the modern banker, control the community's credit, and use it in a dictatorial way, now to make cannons, now to get the community into debt; both despise the individual, both are out to dominate the world. Worship of race, worship of money, a terrified world under the jaws of the death bellowers, a world kneeling under the burden of ruinous and unpayable debentures; bend or break, pay or die.
Prosperity does not depend on a constant favourable or unfavourable trade balance, a monetary instrument does not need gold to play its part. It is the unemployment of money that causes the unemployment of men, and the injection of new money would give new life to our whole activity. With money geared to the needs of the country, it would be possible to protect Canada from recessions.
If the money supply regulated by the government eliminates stagnation, the ownership of money in the hands of the government would direct activities and constitute a real dictatorship of government on the economic life; it would be a replacement of banking dictatorship by government dictatorship.
If, on the contrary, by way of deduction, money originally placed in the hands of consumers controlled the economic life according to the desires of the consumers, it would be a social economic democracy in which freedom would flourish and against which any endeavour of planning or dictatorship would not have any chance.
The policy of your proposed planning- only salaries to workers and interest to sponsors-will never solve this problem, since progress reduces the number of wage-earners, and it is because we hold on to the policy of salaries and interest that thousands and millions of human beings starve to death, cursing progress instead of being thankful for it. That is why Social Credit advocates the distribution of dividends to everyone to enable him to buy his share of progress.
I say his share of progress. Progress is the result of science which, in conjunction with the individual work of the inventor and the sponsor who are rewarded in the normal way, justifies the latter. But accumulated science which is a common wealth, plays an

Economic Council of Canada Important part in invention and progress. So what is left after the capitalist and the inventor, as also the workers, have been rewarded; so it is the share of the accumulated science that belongs to everyone.
That is why all the good things which remain unsold, all the good things salaries and interests do not buy belong to everybody and everybody must be entitled to his share, instead of letting those things deteriorate and stop progress.
And who is to see that everybody gets his share of the progress made? The government, since it is the government that acts for everybody and is responsible for the common good.
There are two ways of enabling people to buy their share of progress. First, by reducing the price of goods so that one may buy more with each dollar; second, by increasing the number of dollars in people's hands.
Progress in the volume of production requires progress in the money supply. Where it is enormous in the first instance, it must also be made enormous in the field of distribution. Those who stick to the old method of financial distribution are enemies of progress as far as distribution goes; they are paralysing the advance of progress in the field of production and are paving the way for the progress of revolution. Just like progress distinguishes man from beast, Social Credit distinguishes the intelligent from the stupid.
The government of a country surely has the right to manage, to legislate, to implement for the good of all, the prosperity of all. The government holds that right or, to put it another way, that judicial power. It also has the physical power, the implementation power, it is capable to find the men, machines and tools needed to serve the community. But it happens that the government does not feel it has the financial power. It is always on the financial side that its action is limited.
That means that even with unchallenged judicial power and almost unlimited physical power, the government is immobilized by the lack of financial power. The same conclusions hold true with regard to centralized, planified government through Bill C-72 dealing with economic planning and submitted in this house by the minister, who is an economist to boot. Judicial and physical powers are not enough without financial power.
The minister is very careful to keep far away from the financial power.
[Mr. Latulippe.l

That is why, while claiming rights for every individual, while requesting the greatest judicial power for the lower bodies, we maintain that unless financial power is also given to individuals, corporations and governments, the economy will remain at a standstill, plans will remain unimplemented, some reports will gather dust because they will not be read-the minister is aware of that-citizens will remain destitute and unemployment will increase.
Budgets will keep on showing deficits, citizens will be taxed more and more, goods will remain on the shelves in spite of urgent needs. Men will remain unemployed next to rusting machines.
We are not against the price of butter rising to enable farmers to show a profit, but the reasons given by the professor of economics are nothing short of capitulation before a set of figures. Adjust the individual, adjust the consumer, adjust demand to supply, always the wrong way: man is sacrificed. When shall we see the bright ones asking for an adjustment of the purchasing power?
To production capacity, money in hand, the consumer orders what he wishes, and as he pays, production adjusts itself to demand as it should, and man remains the master.
The proposed plans and the planned economy will tell us what to produce, what to buy, how much, at what specific time and what are the individual basic needs for this and that. Planned economy will make all individuals and all appetites equal because the great men, who are not equal, will have decided so. Planned economy may be an amusing game for those who play it, for those who plan it. But it is much less attractive for those who are subjected to planning upon whom planning is imposed.
The trouble with monopoly is that power is held by those who control it. Through planning, you are going to replace private monopoly by state monopoly.
That would only mean changing a group of controllers for another one even more important.
The government employees in charge of nationalized industries could dictate the kind of products, the quality of production, the choice of employees, the salaries paid and the selling price of the products.
There is no place for competitive industry which endeavours to please the public better. Only one authority, that of the government, would control production. And if planning and socialization put such a vast and concentrated power in the hands of a political party, what could be done to get rid of it? They

would have the power. It would mean the simultaneous control of industry, finance and policy. And, to administer that tremendous government control, you would have to set up a large government bureaucracy. People may imagine what such bureaucracy would be, considering the one established since the war by the Ottawa government to control industry and business.
The plans conceived by the hon. minister are merely plans to activate production, create methods and increase the yield, so that there is no problem in this respect. The issue is with regard to distribution, and why not take nature as a model.
The sun and the atmosphere function automatically and are only subject to variations due to natural and normal causes. They are giving us the results for which they were created.
The same should be the case with the monetary economic system. It ought to give people the means of buying the fruits they are able to produce. It ought to be such that the consumption of goods equals production, and those results should not entail the danger of so-called sound financing with its pyramids of debts, its usury, taxes and artificial scarcities.
There is only one rule for money: there must be enough to set in action all the legitimate trade. It is bad when there is not enough or too much. If our country can issue one dollar bonds, it can issue one dollar bills as well. The same factors that give value to the bond would do the same for the bill. But there is a difference in that the bond enables the money dealer to be reimbursed twice.
That is how financiers bring about their control without being interfered with while groups tear one another to pieces without solving anything.
It is impossible to solve the dilemma without wiping out the debt-money system. Only Social Credit has the solution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I will take advantage of this unusual generosity on the part of the Secretary of State (Mr. Business of the House Pickersgill) but if, as he has indicated, it is necessary to fill in one or two minutes until it is ten o'clock, then I will proceed to do so.
I was quite interested when I read rather carefully the speech of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) in introducing this measure, in which he said: "Its purpose is to establish economic planning in this country". I have read the bill through with very great care and I can see no possible grounds whatever for this particular deduction. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I was very disappointed this evening. I had hoped to have the opportunity of striking a blow for biculturalism by remarking on the fortunate conjuncture of name and function with regard to the introduction of this bill and then, alas, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue (Mr. Martineau) dealt with it ahead of me. But when I look at the bill itself I can see no reason for the minister's optimistic statement that its purpose is to establish economic planning in this country.
Nowhere in the bill does it suggest that there is to be anyone who is to have the authority to plan. What we are going to have is a number of people who will be asked to compile various statistical data and make economic forecasts; but nowhere is there any suggestion that there is to be any coherent plan produced. In fact I would say this is merely an attempt to correct by unplanned operations the results of planlessness while maintaining the conditions under which planlessness will continue inevitably. It is rather like refusing to take the wheel, but asking passengers to lean first to port and then to starboard in the hope that they may perhaps in some way affect the course of the vessel. Of course, Mr. Speaker, this is very handy when those who are in charge of the navigation appear to be so uncertain as to the destination that should lie at the end of their course.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I call to your attention the fact that it is ten o'clock.

subtopic: LETTER TO PROVINCIAL PREMIERS SUGGESTING CONFERENCE

speechtext:
Ottawa, July 12th, 1963.
(Copy of letter sent to the premiers of all the provinces)
Dear Premier	
The replies that I have so far received to my letter of June 20th indicate that the premiers of the provinces generally look with favour on the suggestion of a federal-provincial conference to discuss matters of mutual interest in the sphere of pensions and related insurance benefits.
It is now expected that the resolution regarding the Canada Pension Plan, which I sent to you with my earlier letter, will be moved in the House of Commons next week. At that time the Minister of National Health and Welfare intends to make a statement fully outlining the government's proposal. Copies of this statement will be sent to you as soon as it is made.
The provinces will therefore shortly have before them the information needed in order that there may be useful federal-provincial discussions about pensions. This is already the case in another matter of interest to the provinces, namely the federal government's proposal to promote increased employment
by financial assistance, in the form of loans with provincial approval, to enable municipalities to augment or accelerate their capital works programmes. This proposal has been set out in detail in the bill which is before the House of Commons.
I think it would be of value to the public, as well as to the governments and others directly concerned, if federal-provincial discussions on these two matters were held as soon as possible.
Accordingly, I am now writing to enquire whether you would be able to attend a two-day conference in Ottawa on July 26th and 27th.
In addition to discussing pensions and this assistance to municipalities, such a meeting would provide opportunity for consideration of the procedure and timing of a full federal-provincial conference later in the year.
I would propose that the conference on July 26th and 27th should be held in camera, though of course each of us would be free before or after to make such public statements as he may wish regarding his government's views on the subjects under discussion.
Yours sincerely, (signed) L. B. Pearson

subtopic: LETTER AND RESOLUTION FROM PREMIER LESAGE
speechtext:
Following my letter to you of June 7, 1963, asking you not to proceed with the establishment of a municipal loans fund until the provincial premiers have had an opportunity to confer among themselves in the matter early in August. I feel I should formally draw your attention to a resolution that was unanimously agreed to in the legislative assembly on June 26.
Herewith is a copy of that document.
I must add that I am sure of expressing the unanimous feeling of the members of the Quebec legislative assembly when I say that they consider as a breach of your promise fully to respect provincial rights, in your management of the affairs of this country, the fact of proceeding unilaterally to establish a municipal loans fund which, according
to your platform, was to be instituted solely in co-operation with the provinces.
Under the circumstances, your attitude forces me, most regretfully, to table this letter forthwith in the legislative assembly.
Please accept, Mr. Prime Minister, the assurance of my regards.
Jean Lesage.

Motion unanimously agreed to."
